title: The Ajna chakra in the destiny matrix: how clarity comes to you

seo.title: Ajna chakra in the destiny matrix: calculation and arcana meanings
seo.description: Ajna chakra in the destiny matrix: how to find its three arcana from a birth date, what each one means and why The High Priestess never appears there.

short: Ajna is the sixth chakra, the “third eye”. In the destiny matrix its theme is perception and understanding: how you make sense of what puzzles you, what makes you want to dig in, and what you feel at the edge of the known. In our table Ajna is the sixth row, between Vishuddha and Sahasrara. Physics is point O on the left ray of the matrix, between the birth day A and point J. Energy is point P on the top ray, between the month B and point K. Emotions are the sum of physics and energy. Any number above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. Ajna has three properties that hardly anyone writes about. Its physics and energy are sums of its neighbours, Sahasrara and Vishuddha. Its energy is the same number that stands in the middle of the talent line. And The High Priestess, the great “intuitive” card of the tarot, never appears in anyone’s Ajna.

sections.h2: Where Ajna sits in the destiny matrix
paragraphs: The destiny matrix is an eight-pointed star made of two squares. Point A (the day of birth) is on the left, B (the month) at the top, C (the year) on the right and D (the sum of the first three) at the bottom. In the middle is the centre, E. A ray runs from each outer point to the centre, and the inner points lie along it. Ajna takes the second point from the edge on the left ray and on the top ray.

So the question “where is Ajna in the destiny matrix” has two answers. On the diagram, it is in the upper-left sector: point O on the day ray and point P on the month ray. In our table, it is the sixth row, just before Sahasrara.

The chakra table is a ladder laid across the points of the diagram. It starts at the outer points on the left and at the top (Sahasrara), converges on the centre (Manipura) and fans back out to the outer points on the right and at the bottom (Muladhara).

The table shows that the three upper chakras sit on two rays. The physics of each lies on the day ray, the energy on the month ray. Sahasrara stands at the very edge, Vishuddha next to the centre, and Ajna halfway between. This in-between position is more than geometry: as you will see, Ajna’s numbers are literally added up from its neighbours.

paragraphs.h3: How to work out Ajna by hand

paragraphs: There is only one rule: any number above 22 is reduced by adding its digits until it is 22 or less. Take 31 March 1993 as an example.
The Ajna row is **12 / 10 / 22**: The Hanged Man, The Wheel of Fortune, The Fool. Gender plays no part in the calculation.

The formulas lead to a curious result. The birth year reaches Ajna only through the centre: physics depends on the day and the centre, energy on the month and the centre. So Ajna has almost no generational pattern. Between dates from the 1940s and the 1990s, the share of each arcanum in physics and energy shifts by no more than 0.3 percentage points. Compare Svadhisthana, where the shares of some cards differ between those decades by almost 10 points.

If another calculator gave you different numbers, check three things. Are the columns in the same order: physics, energy, emotions? Is the year reduced by adding its digits (1993 → 22) rather than by taking a remainder? And does the site use the same diagram? Here the calculation follows Natalia Ladini’s classic matrix with points A–T, while some sites use other formulas for the chakras.

sections.h2: What Ajna is and what it governs
paragraphs: In Sanskrit, ajna means “command” or “order”. The verb it comes from means “to notice, to understand”, and its root is the same one that gives English the word “know”. Two meanings meet in one name: to understand and to receive an instruction.

A detailed description of the chakra appears in the Shat-chakra-nirupana, a sixteenth-century treatise. In 1919 Arthur Avalon translated it into English in his book The Serpent Power. There Ajna is the lotus between the eyebrows, “like the moon, (beautifully white)”, with two petals bearing the letters Ha and Ksha. The next verse says: “Within this Lotus dwells the subtle mind (Manas).” And the commentary explains the name: this is where the ajna, the command of the guru, is received, the command “which is communicated from above”. The familiar blue or violet colour comes from the Western “rainbow” scheme of the chakras; in the treatise the lotus is white.

Among tarot authors, Benebell Wen uses the chakras in Holistic Tarot (2015). In her words, the sixth card of the seven chakras spread gives a sense of how a person thinks: their “clarity of thought, insights, wisdom, reason, and intuition”. Intuition is one word out of five here. That is an important correction to the popular image of Ajna as the chakra of clairvoyance.

In the readings on our site, Ajna’s theme is **perception and understanding**. It is not your level of intelligence and not a gift of foresight, but the route by which clarity reaches you: through a diagram or a trial run, through a teacher or your own experience, through an argument, a pause or a sudden image. And also what you feel while clarity has yet to come.
What Ajna in the matrix does not show: IQ, education, how accurate your hunches are, “psychic powers”, eyesight or physical wellbeing. The numbers describe a way of understanding, not how good it is.

sections.h2: Three numbers, three questions about understanding
paragraphs: **Energy (P): what switches on your interest.** Why you want to dig in at all: a clear structure, depth, novelty, mystery, an honest answer, a project moving forward. Energy decides which questions get your attention. For the rest there is never quite enough, however hard you try.

**Physics (O): how you work things out.** Your working method, what you actually do when faced with something you don’t understand. You draw a diagram, look for a textbook, try it straight away, go off to think alone, ask other people, turn the question upside down.

**Emotions (O + P): what you feel at the edge of the understood.** How you live through uncertainty, a mistake, and the moment the picture comes together: calm, excitement, anxiety, lightness, a jolt. This number is built from the first two, and that makes sense: the feeling depends both on what drew you in and on how you worked it out.
On the site the columns run in the order “physics / energy / emotions”, but they are easier to read starting from energy. First a question hooks you, then you work it out, then the feeling arrives.

**Test it on one puzzle.** Remember the last time you really got to the bottom of something: a new job, a tangled contract, the odd behaviour of someone close. What stopped you from giving up? That is energy. What did you do to work it out? That is physics. What did you feel while the picture wouldn’t come together, and at the moment it did? Those are emotions. Read against one real episode, the three arcana say far more than any reference book.

paragraphs.h3: Where the chain breaks

paragraphs: When people say “I’m slow on the uptake” or “my intuition doesn’t work”, they usually mean one of three failures. Each one falls on its own column.

ul: **“I can’t get into it.”** A failure of energy: the question doesn’t touch what really draws you. Someone with The Hierophant in energy finds it hard to learn without a system and a teacher. Someone with The Fool finds it hard to learn from a set programme where nothing can be asked afresh.

**“I keep going round in circles.”** A failure of physics: the method doesn’t suit the task, or it switches on out of habit. A diagram where a trial step is needed. Endless trials where a diagram is needed. Solitary pondering where one question to someone who knows would do.

**“I understand, but I don’t trust myself.”** A failure of emotions: not knowing feels like a threat. Then the conclusion comes too early, just to end the unpleasant wait. Or it never comes at all, because any conclusion can be challenged.

paragraphs: Your three arcana suggest what each failure looks like in your case. That is why in the full reading the difficulty of each row is drawn from its combination rather than taken from a general list.

sections.h2: Ajna sits between meaning and speech
paragraphs: The chakra table is built so that Ajna’s numbers are sums of its neighbours. This follows directly from the formulas of the method:

ul: **Ajna’s physics = Sahasrara’s physics + Vishuddha’s physics**, because O = A + J;
**Ajna’s energy = Sahasrara’s energy + Vishuddha’s energy**, because P = B + K;
**emotions** are then calculated from Ajna’s own finished numbers: O + P.

paragraphs: Here is how it looks for 31.03.1993:

From here on this is our reading, not a rule of the method. Sahasrara is about what you live for and what matters to you. Vishuddha is about how you express yourself and get your thought across to others. Ajna stands between them, and that is exactly the right place for understanding. A thought cut off from what matters to you hangs in the air. A thought that cannot be spoken stays a vague feeling. Understanding is the moment when what matters becomes clear enough to be put into words.

paragraphs.h3: Ajna’s energy is the middle of the talent line

paragraphs: The talent line in the matrix runs along the top ray: B–P–K. Look closely and you will see that it is the energy column of the three upper chakras: the month B is Sahasrara’s energy, P is Ajna’s energy, K is Vishuddha’s energy. For 31.03.1993 the talent line is 3–10–7, and its middle number, 10, is the same as Ajna’s energy.

In the talent section the middle arcanum is treated as the main one: it shows the form in which the gift unfolds. Our reading: what you are curious to understand and how your gift unfolds are described by one and the same card. That is why work that gives your curiosity nothing to catch on wears you out faster than hard work. If you have already looked at your talent line, you know your Ajna energy: it is the second number.

paragraphs.h3: Ajna’s physics sits on the calling-card ray

paragraphs: Physics O lies on the day ray: A — O — J — E. On the site point A is called the calling card: the first impression you make and your usual way of making contact. Point J is the step from an inner state to visible action. Our image: your way of working things out grows from the same root as your way of meeting people. The way you walk into a new group — straight in, cautiously, with a question, with a plan ready — is often the way you walk into a new task too.

sections.h2: Why The High Priestess never appears in the intuition chakra
paragraphs: The High Priestess is the great “intuitive” card of the tarot. Wen links her with inner knowing, intuition and hidden meaning. Yet she turns up in nobody’s Ajna, in any of the three columns. The Magician never appears there either.

The reason is arithmetic. Every Ajna number is the sum of two arcana: physics of the day and point J, energy of the month and point K, emotions of physics and energy. Here such sums are never less than four, and reducing the numbers from 23 to 44 gives 3 to 12. The numbers 1 and 2 have nowhere to come from.

The High Priestess lives one floor up, in Sahasrara. In Sahasrara’s physics she appears for people born on the 2nd of any month, in its energy for those born in February, and in its emotions only for those born on 1 January.

Waite gives this arithmetic some unexpected support. In the divinatory meanings of the Major Arcana he uses the word “intuition” once, and not for The High Priestess. Her list reads: “Secrets, mystery, the future as yet unrevealed… silence, tenacity; mystery, wisdom, science.” “Intuition” stands in the list for The Hanged Man: “Wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice, intuition, divination, prophecy.” The Hanged Man does appear in Ajna, though rarely. In each of the three columns it is among the three rarest arcana, and in the Ajna row as a whole it turns up in roughly one calculation in twelve.

The most frequent arcanum in Ajna is The Hierophant. It comes first in both physics (8.7%) and energy (7.3%). Waite set it beside The High Priestess as her opposite: she is the hidden, inner side of a teaching, he is the open side, handed on through school and teacher. Frequency is a property of the calendar, not a verdict. But the picture is telling: in Ajna the matrix describes not knowledge out of nowhere but a path to understanding.

In his chapter on divination Waite himself writes that the value of intuition “is of course assumed”, and adds: “Where intuition fails, or is absent, concentration, intellectual observation and deduction must be used to the fullest extent… But intuition, even if apparently dormant, may be cultivated by practice.” And further: “it becomes possible with practice to distinguish between a guess of the conscious mind and an impression arising from the mind which is sub-conscious.” That is a good description of how Ajna works in the matrix. Its business is not miracles but telling things apart: a guess from knowledge, what was seen from what was filled in.
There are three cards where Waite speaks directly about sight. All three can appear in Ajna, in any column:

ul: **The Moon**: “The intellectual light is a reflection and beyond it is the unknown mystery which it cannot shew forth.”
**The Sun**: the light of consciousness here is “the direct as the antithesis of the reflected light”.
**Judgement**: “let those who have inward eyes look and discover therewith”.

paragraphs: Is there a Hanged Man, a Moon or a Hierophant in your Ajna? The calculator shows all three numbers in a second, along with the other six chakras.

sections.h2: Reading your Ajna: the meanings of arcana 3 to 22
paragraphs: Find each of your numbers in the right column. Under the name is the arcanum’s theme in Ajna, then how it sounds in each of the three roles. Every card has a side where it helps you understand and a side where it starts to get in the way. Both are given. Shares are calculated across all birth dates from 1940 to 2012.

paragraphs.h3: 3 · The Empress — understanding that grows

paragraphs: In Waite, The Empress is “the outer sense of the Word”, but “she does not herself carry its interpretation”. The second, hidden sense of the Word is written on The High Priestess’s scroll. For Ajna this is a precise hint: the image is born easily, but it still has to be given a meaning.

ul: **Physics.** A thought grows gradually, out of observations and examples: a sketch, a mock-up, a living picture you can touch. You understand when you see an idea bear fruit. Shadow: growing a version so generously that it hurts to cut it back later.

**Energy.** Interest switches on at the chance to grow a design out of details and join observations into a living whole. Shadow: admiring the growth more than checking whether it is heading the right way.
**Emotions.** Joy when a thought sprouts and a whole harvest of ideas rises from a single guess. Shadow: disappointment when the harvest has to be thinned out for the sake of a result.

paragraphs.h3: 4 · The Emperor — understanding with a frame

paragraphs: Waite raises The Emperor to “the intellectual throne”, to “the lordship of thought”, and in the divinatory list names “reason, conviction”. The caveat is his too: this is not yet “the wisdom which draws from a higher world”. In Ajna’s energy and emotions The Emperor is the rarest arcanum (3.3% and 2.2%).

ul: **Physics.** A diagram, stages, key concepts: the frame first, then the details. With your explanation someone else can go through it step by step. Shadow: the diagram keeps growing until it mostly explains itself.

**Energy.** A need to understand how a thing is built and to know the limits of the question: interest holds while it is clear what belongs inside. Shadow: an awkward fact gets filed under “exceptions” and “I’ll sort it out later”.
**Emotions.** Confidence when everything is in its place. Shadow: irritation at facts that break a neat picture.

paragraphs.h3: 5 · The Hierophant — understanding through a school

paragraphs: The most frequent arcanum in Ajna: it turns up in 8.7% of calculations in physics and 7.3% in energy. Among the card’s meanings Waite lists “the man to whom the Querent has recourse”.

ul: **Physics.** Learning by a proven method, from a master, through a recognised programme, checking your thinking against the canon. Shadow: the authority of the source takes the place of understanding its argument.
**Energy.** A pull towards tested knowledge and a coherent teaching, a wish to belong to a school. Shadow: something new is accepted only once others have accepted it.
**Emotions.** Calm when an explanation is clear and shared with others. Shadow: confusion when two recognised systems contradict each other.

paragraphs.h3: 6 · The Lovers — understanding through choice

paragraphs: Wen sees in this card a choice in which heart and reason may fail to agree. In Ajna it becomes a way of understanding through comparison and agreement.

ul: **Physics.** You understand by comparing: two paths, the one chosen and the one turned down, an argument and what your heart tells you. Shadow: weighing things up forever so as not to choose.

**Energy.** Thinking together with someone close, opening your train of thought to each other. What you love is what you understand best. Shadow: checking your opinion against someone else’s until your own falls silent.
**Emotions.** Head and heart in agreement: the right answer feels like recognition. Shadow: awkwardness when your understanding parts ways with the choice of someone close.

paragraphs.h3: 7 · The Chariot — understanding on the move

paragraphs: Waite writes of “triumph in the mind”, but with a caveat: the liberation the charioteer brings “may leave himself in the bondage of the logical understanding”.

ul: **Physics.** Testing an idea in action straight away, checking a version on the move and adjusting it along the way. Shadow: a conclusion before the task is understood.
**Energy.** The thrill of progress: whatever moves things forward is interesting. Shadow: dropping a question that gives no quick headway.
**Emotions.** The thrill of a move found and a puzzle cracked. Shadow: frustration when understanding requires standing still.

paragraphs.h3: 8 · Justice — understanding by a fair measure

paragraphs: The most frequent arcanum in Ajna’s emotions, at 8.5% of calculations. Waite’s divinatory list has “Equity, rightness, probity”. He himself made this card the eleventh, swapping it with Strength, though he admitted that Justice is “usually numbered eight”.

ul: **Physics.** Hearing both sides, weighing the inconvenient argument, looking for a refutation of your favourite version. Shadow: a trial instead of understanding.
**Energy.** A need for honest grounds and one measure for every argument. Shadow: demanding proof where there can be none.
**Emotions.** Relief at a fair outcome. Shadow: no peace until every side has been taken into account.

paragraphs.h3: 9 · The Hermit — understanding you reach yourself

paragraphs: The Hermit’s beacon, according to Waite, says “where I am, you also may be.” The light is held up so that others can see it.

ul: **Physics.** Working things out alone, in silence, step by step, testing them on yourself. Shadow: letting no one near your reasoning until it is ready.

**Energy.** A need to reach the heart of the matter yourself and understand it to the very bottom. Shadow: depth for its own sake, as the question sinks into navel-gazing while circumstances make the decision for you.
**Emotions.** The quiet joy of a conclusion of your own. Shadow: an understanding you never shared.

paragraphs.h3: 10 · The Wheel of Fortune — understanding repeats and turns

paragraphs: In Waite the sphinx on the Wheel stands for “stability amidst movement”. In Ajna this is the ability to see a pattern where others see chance.

ul: **Physics.** Noticing repeats and turning points, seeing events as a change of seasons, separating your own part from circumstances. Shadow: explaining everything with “that’s just how it turned out”.
**Energy.** Interest in the patterns inside change and in unexpected connections. Shadow: every piece of news stirs you up, and the picture never has time to settle.
**Emotions.** A lift at a turning point, joy at a connection found. Shadow: unease when the picture changes faster than you can make sense of it.

paragraphs.h3: 11 · Strength — understanding without force

paragraphs: Waite rejects ordinary “self-confidence” as an explanation of this card: for him it is the higher nature, which tames the passions gently.

ul: **Physics.** Patiently working through the uncomfortable, calmly hearing out someone else’s argument, digging without accusing. Shadow: putting up with uncertainty longer than it deserves.
**Energy.** Gentle persistence: attention holds for a long time and doesn’t snap into a first reaction. Shadow: not letting go of a question it is time to drop.
**Emotions.** Calm in the face of a crack in the picture, confidence once it has been worked through. Shadow: keeping a straight face when you are in fact afraid of not understanding.

paragraphs.h3: 12 · The Hanged Man — understanding from the other side

paragraphs: The only card of the Major Arcana for which Waite names intuition among the divinatory meanings. The hanged man’s face, he says, expresses “deep entrancement, not suffering”. In Ajna The Hanged Man is rare in every column: 2.4% in physics, 3.5% in energy, 2.5% in emotions.

ul: **Physics.** Turning the question over: looking at it from your opponent’s place, from a student’s, from the end of the road. Shadow: hanging over a question when it is time to act.
**Energy.** A readiness to give up a quick conclusion and step away from the question for a while. Shadow: “I’ll think about it some more” becomes a way of not deciding.
**Emotions.** Calmly staying with no answer. Shadow: getting so used to suspension that the answer is no longer needed.

paragraphs.h3: 13 · Death — understanding that renews itself

paragraphs: Waite writes of the mystical death, entered while still in this life, as “a change in the form of consciousness”. Nothing could fit Ajna better. In physics it is the rarest arcanum: 2.25%.

ul: **Physics.** Closing down refuted models, honestly admitting that a version has had its day. Shadow: throwing out an explanation before it has been tested.
**Energy.** A readiness to relearn, a pull towards renewing what you know. Shadow: the new carries you off, and the old is left half thought through.
**Emotions.** Relief and sadness as you part with an earlier conclusion. Shadow: mourning for too long a version you put a lot into.

paragraphs.h3: 14 · Temperance — understanding blended from different sources

paragraphs: In Waite this card “tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures” of a person.

ul: **Physics.** Bringing sources together, stitching pieces of evidence, joining impressions with facts. Shadow: a compromise where a choice is needed.
**Energy.** Combining calculation with instinct and theory with practice, fitting the method to the task. Shadow: endless fine-tuning instead of a result.
**Emotions.** Evenness in the face of the unclear, a calm attitude to exceptions. Shadow: smoothing over a contradiction that deserved a closer look.

paragraphs.h3: 15 · The Devil — understanding that takes hold

paragraphs: On Waite’s card the chained figures have animal tails, “but there is human intelligence in the faces”. And the one above them is “not to be their master for ever”.

ul: **Physics.** Noticing what holds people: profit, weaknesses, the bait they fall for. Seeing the chains even at the top and noticing your own stake in a conclusion. Shadow: looking for a catch in everything.
**Energy.** Being gripped by a question: a thought you can’t tear yourself away from. Shadow: the thought starts to hold you.
**Emotions.** A strong attachment to your own version. Shadow: it is hard to give up a conclusion even when it has stopped explaining anything.

paragraphs.h3: 16 · The Tower — understanding that tests foundations

paragraphs: Waite sees in The Tower a ruin of the mind rather than of matter, “destruction on the intellectual side”: “the rending of a House of Doctrine… the reference is, however, to a House of Falsehood”.

ul: **Physics.** Checking the starting assumption, looking for the false support, testing an idea to breaking point. Shadow: breaking things before you have checked them.
**Energy.** The thrill of finding what everything rests on. Shadow: interest only where something is falling apart.
**Emotions.** A sudden insight, the shock of a mismatch. Shadow: after the jolt it is hard to trust even what is true.

paragraphs.h3: 17 · The Star — understanding that sees what is possible

paragraphs: Waite sees in the figure of The Star the Great Mother in the “supernal Understanding” of the Kabbalah, who gives to the spheres below “in the measure that they can receive her influx”. He links The High Priestess with the same supernal Understanding, but of these two cards only The Star ever appears in Ajna.

ul: **Physics.** Sketching the future, seeing a possibility that is not yet visible. Shadow: a beautiful image of the future instead of a check.
**Energy.** A pull towards prospects still out of sight, inspiration from generously shared knowledge. Shadow: hoping clarity will come by itself.
**Emotions.** Hope in the face of the unknown, inspiration from what is possible. Shadow: disappointment when reality turns out paler than the sketch.

paragraphs.h3: 18 · The Moon — understanding half-tones

paragraphs: For Waite The Moon is “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit”. The path on the card leads into the unknown, and only reflected light shows the way.

ul: **Physics.** Catching shades, hints, things left unsaid. Telling what you saw from what you filled in. Shadow: filling it in.
**Energy.** The pull of mystery, a sensitivity to what is hidden. Shadow: the unclear attracts you more than the clear.
**Emotions.** A vague unease and an active imagination at the edge of the understood. Shadow: mistaking anxiety for intuition.

paragraphs.h3: 19 · The Sun — understanding in direct light

paragraphs: Waite explains the child on The Sun as “a child in the sense of simplicity and innocence in the sense of wisdom”.

ul: **Physics.** Putting the essence simply, showing it in daylight, with no dark corners. Shadow: simplifying until it is no longer true.
**Energy.** A wish to see the whole picture clearly, for yourself and for others. Shadow: a dislike of questions that have no simple answer.
**Emotions.** Joy at a simple, clear answer. In this column The Sun is uncommon: 2.8%. Shadow: impatience with the half-dark you sometimes have to walk through.

paragraphs.h3: 20 · Judgement — understanding what you have lived through

paragraphs: Waite asks: “What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response — almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye?”

ul: **Physics.** Reviewing the road behind you, looking back honestly, gathering all the evidence. Shadow: reviewing the past without end.
**Energy.** Interest in where it all led, the call of lived experience. Shadow: searching the past for an answer about the future.
**Emotions.** Clarity as an awakening, an inner “this is it”. Shadow: the insight demands an immediate response and leaves no time to check it.

paragraphs.h3: 21 · The World — understanding the whole

paragraphs: Waite’s World is “the perfection and end of the Cosmos”. In Ajna it is the need to see how all the parts fit together.

ul: **Physics.** Holding the whole system in mind, bringing different sides into one picture. Shadow: the picture matters more than the details that don’t fit it.
**Energy.** A need to grasp how the whole is built. Shadow: not starting until you can see all of it.
**Emotions.** Joy at a whole that has come together. Shadow: in time a neat system starts explaining yesterday.

paragraphs.h3: 22 · The Fool — a beginner’s understanding

paragraphs: Waite’s Fool has a face “full of intelligence and expectant dream”. This is not foolishness but “the spirit in search of experience”.

ul: **Physics.** Taking on the unfamiliar as a beginner, testing by trying rather than by arguing, asking about the simplest things. Shadow: giving up at the trial stage.
**Energy.** Freedom from “that’s how it has always been done” and “I already know what he’s like”. Shadow: doubting everything and asserting nothing.
**Emotions.** Lightness in the face of the unfamiliar, the joy of not knowing. Shadow: the beginner’s position as a hiding place, with the conclusion put off again and again.

paragraphs: The table of meanings gives you words, but not the meaning of a row. The Hanged Man in physics next to The Wheel in energy means one thing; next to The Moon, something quite different. You can see how in the examples below.

**One card in two columns.** Physics matches energy in 20 rows, from 3-3-6 to 22-22-8. This happens slightly more often than once in twelve calculations. It is not a doubling of the quality. In energy the card describes what makes you want to work something out, in physics how you go about it. For these people the way they think coincides with what they like to think about, so what they feel at the edge of the understood matters all the more. This is how it sounds in the full reading for row 4-4-8: “The Emperor appears here twice, and he works differently each time. In the way you handle information he is a method: gather the facts, put each one in its place, see what follows from what. In your energy he becomes a motive — you are fed by the right to bring order to your understanding yourself, rather than accept someone else’s ready-made conclusion. Justice shapes how clarity feels: a conclusion satisfies you when everything has been honestly taken into account, including the inconvenient parts.”

**Mirror rows and The Moon.** Add 18 to any number from 5 to 11, reduce the sum, and you get the same number back: 7 + 18 = 25 → 7. That is why Ajna has twelve rows where emotions repeat the neighbouring card. These are X-18-X, with The Moon in energy, and 18-X-X, with The Moon in physics. Such a row falls to about one date in 27. In Waite The Moon is the card of reflected light, and in arithmetic it behaves the same way: it reflects the number beside it. Our reading: for these people the feeling at the edge of the understood is a reflection of their way of working things out, or of their interest, seen in half-light.

**The most and the least common.** Ajna has 336 possible rows in all. Across all dates from 1940 to 2012, the most common is 10-10-20, about once in 117 dates. Next come 11-11-22, 9-11-20, 8-10-18 and 11-9-20. At the other end are the one-offs:

ul: **4-22-8** falls to a single date in two hundred years, from 1900 to 2100: 18 September 2000. That date’s year arcanum is 2, and in these two centuries only the year 2000 has that digit sum.
**21-14-8** and **20-9-11** last appeared in 1940, on 18 January and 17 July, and will not return until 2039. Nobody born between 1941 and 2038 has them.
**20-21-5** appeared on 17 April 1943, 1952, 1961 and 1970, and will next appear in 2069.

paragraphs: Even 4-22-8 has its own text in the full reading. It is called “Curiosity that carries a map”.
Take the same date, 31.03.1993. The Ajna row is The Hanged Man, The Wheel of Fortune, The Fool.

ol: **Energy — The Wheel of Fortune.** Interest is switched on by change: what has shifted, what keeps repeating, where a turn has come.

**Physics — The Hanged Man.** Working things out here means stopping and looking from the other side. In Waite the tree the man hangs from is “living wood”, and his face expresses absorption, not torment.
**Emotions — The Fool.** At the edge of the understood there is lightness: you may not yet know how it all works and still give it a try.
**One connecting thought.** When the old answer stops working, you are able to see a different move.

paragraphs: This is how the row looks in the full reading:
**Finding a way out where there was a dead end**

head: Position

rows: Seeing it from the other side

paragraphs: Sometimes a solution comes into view only after you stop pushing for the old answer. In Ajna, the chakra of mind and understanding, The Hanged Man brings this kind of pause: the habitual view loosens its grip for a while. The Wheel of Fortune reminds you that circumstances may already have changed. And The Fool lets you meet the unfamiliar with curiosity — not yet knowing how it all works, and still trying to figure it out. **Your opportunity here is to see a different move.** Say a piece of work stalls at the same stage time after time. At first you just want to push harder. But a look from the outside reveals something else: the people involved each understand the result differently. So instead of yet another push, a clear agreement appears. The understanding of the task itself changes — and what seemed impossible to get past finally gives way. The flip side is falling in love with a new explanation too quickly. A moment ago everything seemed clear, but then something else happened — and the old picture fell apart. The next version is just as captivating, and you want to start over. If no idea has time to meet experience, thinking turns into one endless house move: every place is interesting, none is lived in. Clarity comes when a new view is carried on into action.

Notice where the difficulty came from. It is not in any of the cards on its own. The Hanged Man can let go of the old view, The Wheel notices that everything has already changed, The Fool happily starts again. All three pull towards a new explanation, and none of them holds on to the old one long enough to test it in action.

paragraphs.h3: One energy, four ways of understanding

paragraphs: The Moon turns up in Ajna’s energy in roughly one calculation in twenty. It is a pull towards the unsaid and the hidden. But what a person with that pull actually does is decided by the neighbouring cards.

paragraphs: The Hermit follows the unclear alone, by his own lantern, until he reaches the bottom. The Fool doesn’t guess but takes a small step and watches what happens, while The Emperor in emotions brings calm once the mystery has a firm outline. Strength tests a hunch with a calm question, and uncertainty doesn’t frighten it. The Hanged Man shifts the angle, and the puzzle opens up through an image from which, as with The Empress, a harvest of ideas grows. The same Moon, four different minds. That is why the reading of a single arcanum can never replace the reading of a row.

sections.h2: Your Ajna and the other six chakras
paragraphs: Seven chakras, three arcana in each: physics, energy, emotions. The numbers appear straight after the free calculation. The interpretations open in the full reading; until you pay, the rows are locked.

Ajna is one row out of seven, and it has the closest ties to its neighbours. Its physics and energy are built from Sahasrara and Vishuddha, and its energy also stands in the middle of the talent line. In the matrix, understanding does not live on its own: it grows out of what matters to you and is tested by what you can put into words.
The full chakra reading for your date contains:

ul: **seven sections, from Muladhara to Sahasrara**, each with its own title, main idea and captions for the three arcana: the role each card plays in that chakra;

**three connected paragraphs per chakra**: the chakra’s theme and what each card brings to it, a picture of how the combination looks in life, and the difficulty that grows out of the same combination;

**a separate text for each of Ajna’s 336 possible rows**: not three dictionary meanings glued together, but a reading of that exact combination, including the row that fell to a single date in two hundred years;
**a summary, “What matters most for you”**: the thread that ties the seven chakras into one portrait, and the main tension in your chart.

sections.h2: “Opening the third eye”: what Ajna really shows
paragraphs: A great deal is written about the third eye: how to “open” it, the signs that it is “closed”, which numbers give “strong intuition”. The destiny matrix cannot be read that way.

ul: **The numbers are names of arcana, not scores.** 22 is not stronger than 3, The Moon does not make anyone clairvoyant, and The Emperor does not block intuition. There is no such thing as an empty Ajna: everyone has three cards in it.
**“Plus” and “minus” are not different arcana but two modes of the same one.** Your way of understanding and its typical trap grow from one root. The trap begins where a strength goes too far.

paragraphs: So instead of “how do I open my Ajna?” it is more useful to ask: where does my way of understanding slip into its shadow? In the full reading the third paragraph of every chakra is about exactly that shift, and it is written for your combination, not for the arcanum in general.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation**: Natalia Ladini’s classic destiny matrix with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, J = A + E, K = B + E, Ajna’s physics O = A + J, energy P = B + K, emotions = O + P. Every sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. All the numerical facts — the 336 possible rows, the absence of 1 and 2, the match between energy and the talent line, the frequencies of arcana and rows, the single date for row 4-22-8 — come from running through every date from 1900 to 2100. Shares are given for all birth dates from 1940 to 2012.

**Card meanings**: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922), including the divinatory meanings and the chapter on divination in Part III, and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), the chapter on the Seven Chakras spread. Quotations are given in the authors’ original English.
**Tradition**: the Shat-chakra-nirupana in Arthur Avalon’s translation (The Serpent Power, 1919), verses 32–33 with commentary.

Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the destiny matrix. The physics / energy / emotions columns, the meanings of the arcana in Ajna, and the links with Sahasrara, Vishuddha and the talent line are the author’s interpretation.

This is a symbolic model for self-observation, not a forecast and not a medical description. The numbers say nothing about intelligence, eyesight, physical condition or supernatural abilities, and they do not decide whether anyone’s chakras are “open”.

paragraphs: **Find out how clarity comes to you.** Enter your date of birth and you will see the three arcana of your Ajna and of the other six chakras straight away. In the full reading each of the seven chakras is read as a whole: what matters to you, how it looks in life, and where a strength turns into a trap.

intro: You will see the three arcana of your Ajna straight after the calculation by date of birth, free and with no sign-up. The other six chakras will be right beside them.

faq.q: Where is Ajna in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: In the upper-left sector of the diagram. Physics is point O on the day ray, second from the edge, between the birth day A and point J. Energy is point P on the month ray, also second from the edge, between the month B and point K. Emotions are their sum and have no point of their own on the diagram. In our table Ajna is the sixth row, between Vishuddha and Sahasrara.

faq.q: How do I calculate Ajna from my date of birth?
faq.a: You need the day arcanum A, the month B and the year arcanum C, which is the sum of the year’s digits. Work out D = A + B + C and the centre E = A + B + C + D. Then J = A + E and K = B + E. Physics = A + J, energy = B + K, emotions = physics + energy. Anything above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. For 31.03.1993, for example, you get 12 / 10 / 22.

faq.q: I have The Moon or The Hanged Man in Ajna. Does that mean strong intuition?
faq.a: No, and the opposite does not follow either. The Moon describes a sensitivity to the unsaid and to images at the edge of the understood, which still have to be told apart from guesses. The Hanged Man is a way of understanding by changing the angle. Waite names intuition only among The Hanged Man’s meanings, but even that card is no measure of a gift. How far your guesses turn into understanding is shown by the whole row, not by a single card.

faq.q: Why do The High Priestess and The Magician never appear in Ajna?
faq.a: Because of arithmetic. Every Ajna number is the sum of two arcana, and here that sum is never less than four. Reducing the numbers from 23 to 44 gives 3 to 12. So 1 and 2 never come up in anyone’s Ajna. The High Priestess appears one floor up, in Sahasrara: for people born on the 2nd of a month, in February or on 1 January.

faq.q: Are Ajna’s energy and the talent line the same thing?
faq.a: The number is the same: Ajna’s energy always equals the middle number of the talent line B–P–K, because both come from point P. But the roles differ. In the talent line P shows the form in which your gift unfolds. In Ajna it shows what switches on your interest in understanding. The match means that what you are curious to understand and how your gift unfolds are described by one and the same card.

faq.q: How can I tell if my Ajna is “closed”?
faq.a: Not from the numbers. An arcanum’s number is the name of a symbol, not a score, and everyone has all three columns filled. What popular readings call a “closed” Ajna is usually one of three failures: I can’t get into it, I keep going round in circles, I understand but don’t trust myself. It is more useful to find out which column your chain breaks on.

faq.q: Is Ajna different for men and women?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation, so a man and a woman born on the same date have the same numbers. Nor does the reading split understanding into “female intuition” and “male logic”: any card can appear in anyone’s Ajna.

The numbers don’t change: they come from your date of birth. What changes is how you use them. The Emperor can build a diagram that explains the task, or defend the diagram against the task. The Moon can hear what is left unsaid, or fill it in. The Fool can ask the question that shifts everything, or hide in not knowing. The row shows both the trap and the strength of one and the same way of understanding.
